full_judgment: 5. The main contention of Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed centres round the question of separation of the jama by the Pre-emptors it has been contended that the pre-emptors, after their purchase of 22 ½  decimals of lands from the original owner Saralabala Pal in 1969, filed an application before the Revenue-officer for separation of their jama whereupon a Separation Case, bearing No. 605/69-70, was started which ended in an order separating the jama whereupon the two parties paid rents separately. If this is a fact, then, certainly the Pre-emptors ceased to be co-sharers and are debarred from claiming pre-emption. But there is neither any specific finding by any of the three Courts including the High Court Division on this question, nor is there any sufficient evidence on record to determine it. Paradoxically the question as to separation of jama was first raised, not by the Pre-emptee, but by the Pre-emptors themselves in their applications for pre-emption. They stated there that they mutated their names by separating the jama by filing Separation Case No. 605/69-70. Treating this as an admission, the pre-emptee built up her case as the separation of the jama resulting in the Pre-emptors ceasing to be co-sharers in the original jama. Excepting this statement which is apparently an admission against the interest of its maker, there is no evidence that the jama was actually separated and the lands were recorded under separate khatians. The copy of a proposed khatian, No 997/1 , has been produced before us by the appellant-pre-emptee at the time of hearing of the appeals. It shows that a proposal was under consideration of the Revenue-officer for opening up a separate khatian in favour of the respondents in respect of an area of 30 ½  decimals comprising both plot Nos. 329 and 332; but whether the proposal was finally accepted resulting in separation of the jama and payment of rents separately by the two co-sharers, no evidence has been led in this case. So far as the Pre-emptors are concerned, they are not expected to adduce any evidence in this matter as this will certainly go against them. As to why they filed the Separation case, they have now explained that by filing the Separation case only mutation of their names in place of the original owner Sarala Bala Pal was intended and that the proposal for mutation was erroneously referred to "as separation of the jama" and further, that the said case did not reach its finality; consequently, they continued to be co-sharers. As to the Pre-emptee, as already stated above, she also did not produce any evidence but solely depended upon the (admission' of the other party. 'Admission' is no doubt a strong evidence against its maker, but it is also open to him to adduce evidence to show that it is not in fact an "admission' but is the result of bonafide mistake of fact. The appellate Court left the issue undecided by a simple observation that "since the onus lies on the petitioner (Pre-emptor) to prove it and he failed to prove it the benefit of doubt goes to the O.P. (Pre-emptee)". The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division held that it was a case of mutation, but at the same time observed that "since the Pre-emptors were owners of only a part of the land but claimed mutation for the whole of it, it was not a case of mutation at all". In the circumstances, it is found that this all-important question as to separation of the jama-whether the pre-emptors are co-sharers in the land, in other words, whether the jama has been actually separated and rent paid separately has not been decided by any of the Courts. Upon determination of this question the fate of the two pre-emption proceedings depends, and this question should better be determined by the lower Appellate Court.
